title: Velocity-dependent drag and terminal motion
objective: Form and check a linear-drag differential equation, interpret its time constant, and distinguish terminal motion from free fall.
why: A force can depend on the motion it changes. Drag therefore leads naturally to a differential equation rather than a constant-acceleration shortcut. You will derive and verify a complete motion model, preserve initial conditions, compare two drag laws, and explain which limiting statements are physically meaningful.

prerequisites.label: Motion and relative velocity in three dimensions
Differentiation and integration preparation
prerequisites.note: The calculus course is under construction. The needed exponential derivative and definite integral are explained here; the linked free calculus course offers additional preparation.

prerequisites.label: Exponential functions and growth factors
prerequisites.note: Review multiplicative change and exponential decay before interpreting a time constant.

prerequisites.label: Logarithms as inverse functions
prerequisites.note: Review inverse operations and positive logarithm inputs before solving for a drag-model time.

sections.heading: State the force model and the fluid frame
paragraphs: Choose a one-dimensional vertical coordinate with downward positive. Let g≥0 be the downward gravitational magnitude and m>0 the constant mass. We first assume a stationary fluid, a positive constant linear-drag coefficient b, no buoyancy, no contact forces, and constant gravity over the region modeled. The drag force is Fd=-bv, so it opposes the signed velocity relative to the stationary fluid.

Newton's second law becomes $m\,dv/dt=mg-bv$. Acceleration is $a=g-(b/m)v$, which changes as velocity changes. Constant-acceleration position formulas are therefore not generally valid over the drag transient. The equation connects the current velocity to its instantaneous rate of change.

If the fluid moves uniformly at velocity u in the same axes, the linear drag is $F_d=-b(v-u)$. Subtract fluid velocity before selecting a drag direction. A tailwind moving faster than a body can produce drag in the same direction as the body's laboratory velocity, while still opposing its relative motion through the fluid.

Linear drag is an approximation appropriate to some flow conditions, such as sufficiently slow viscous flow around small objects. A speed-squared model is useful in other regimes. Speed alone does not establish validity: size, shape, fluid properties, and flow behavior also matter. Our coefficient is a supplied model parameter, not a claimed measurement for a particular object.

sections.heading: Find the equilibrium velocity and its time scale
paragraphs: For b>0, set acceleration to zero in the force equation: mg-bvT=0. The selected terminal velocity is $v_T=mg/b$. With g>0 it is positive and downward. Both weight and drag are nonzero there; their vector sum is zero. Position continues changing at constant velocity.

The coefficient b has units kg/s because force divided by velocity gives $(\mathrm{kg\,m/s^2})/(\mathrm{m/s})$. The quantity $\tau=m/b$ has units of seconds and is called the time constant. Rewriting the equation gives $dv/dt=(v_T-v)/\tau$.

Below terminal velocity, acceleration is positive; above it, acceleration is negative. The same equilibrium attracts both types of initial state in this constant-coefficient model. A body launched upward has v<0, so drag and gravity both point downward until the velocity reaches zero.

At fixed b and g, multiplying mass by a factor multiplies both vT and τ by that factor. This is a conditional comparison: changing a real object's mass by changing its size may also change its drag coefficient. If g=0 and b>0, the selected terminal velocity is zero, while the positive time constant still describes damping.

sections.heading: Derive the exponential while preserving the initial condition
paragraphs: Let w=v-vT, the signed difference from equilibrium. Since vT is constant, $dw/dt=-w/\tau$. For a nonzero initial difference w0=v0-vT, separation gives $dw/w=-dt/\tau$. Integrating from the initial state yields $\ln|w/w_0|=-t/\tau$. The logarithm acts on a dimensionless ratio, not a velocity with units.

Exponentiating and retaining the initial sign gives $w=w_0e^{-t/\tau}$, so the full solution is $v(t)=v_T+(v_0-v_T)e^{-t/\tau}$. At t=0 the exponential is one and the formula gives v0. At long times the exponential tends to zero and v approaches vT.

The special initial state w0=0 cannot be divided by in the separation step. Check it directly: v(t)=vT is a constant solution. The final formula includes that solution because its transient coefficient is zero. A derivation should preserve an equilibrium solution rather than lose it through division.

The exponential e^z is the function whose derivative is itself; by the chain rule, the derivative of e^(-t/τ) is -(1/τ)e^(-t/τ). The natural logarithm ln is its inverse. Use an exp or e^x key for the exponential and ln for this logarithm. Generated numerical questions accept the calculated decimal value, not a typed exp(...) expression.

sections.heading: Verify the equation as well as the initial value
paragraphs: Differentiating the solution gives $a(t)=-(v_0-v_T)e^{-t/\tau}/\tau$. Independently substituting v(t) into g-(b/m)v gives the same expression, because g=vT/τ. This agreement checks the differential equation; evaluating v(0)=v0 separately checks the initial condition.

A function can satisfy the equation while representing the wrong initial state. For example, changing the transient coefficient changes v(0) without changing the differential equation. Conversely, a function can start from the correct value while using an incorrect decay rate. Passing only one check is insufficient.

For release from rest with g>0, $v=v_T(1-e^{-t/\tau})$ and $a=ge^{-t/\tau}$. Initial acceleration is g because initial drag is zero. Acceleration decreases as the growing drag offsets more of the weight. Terminal motion is not the same as free fall without drag.

For finite t and a nonzero initial difference, the exact exponential is positive, so v does not cross its equilibrium value. It approaches that value asymptotically. Numerical rounding can display a terminal-looking value at a finite time; distinguish that display resolution from exact equality. If the initial velocity equals vT, equilibrium holds from the start.

sections.heading: Integrate velocity to obtain position
paragraphs: With y(0)=y0, integrate the velocity from zero to t. The result is $y(t)=y_0+v_Tt+(v_0-v_T)\tau(1-e^{-t/\tau})$. Each added term has units of length. At t=0 both displacement terms vanish, so the position initial condition is preserved.

For release from rest at y0=0, this becomes $y=v_T[t-\tau(1-e^{-t/\tau})]$. The bracket has units of time. Using y=vTt from the beginning would overestimate the displacement because the body initially moves more slowly than terminal velocity.

Differentiating the position formula recovers the complete velocity expression. This is a useful independent check of the integration sign. For an upward launch, displacement is initially negative in our downward-positive coordinate; it is not a nonnegative distance traveled.

The ideal model does not specify a ground surface or a finite container. If an application includes a landing height, solve for the first admissible contact time and stop or replace the model there. A calculation that extends the mathematical trajectory for many time constants does not prove that a real object has enough unobstructed space to do so.

sections.heading: Read the time constant as a fractional transient
paragraphs: The ratio $(v-v_T)/(v_0-v_T)=e^{-t/\tau}$ describes the remaining fraction of the initial velocity difference, when that difference is nonzero. After one time constant, about 36.8% remains. A body released from rest has therefore gained about 63.2% of its terminal velocity, not 100%.

For release from rest toward a positive terminal velocity, reaching a fraction f with 0<f<1 requires $t=-\tau\ln(1-f)$. The logarithm is negative, making the time positive. A larger target fraction takes longer; f=1 has no finite solution for this non-equilibrium release.

At two, three, and five time constants, the gained fractions are approximately 86.5%, 95.0%, and 99.3%. These are consequences of the exponential, not separate empirical laws. The target-fraction statement assumes a positive terminal value; dividing by vT is inappropriate when g=0 and vT=0.

Plotting against dimensionless time t/τ helps compare different masses and drag coefficients. Equal values of t/τ give equal remaining fractions of the initial difference, while the dimensional velocities and accelerations may differ. Keep dimensional scale and normalized fraction separate when explaining a comparison.

sections.heading: Compare a quadratic law without losing direction or units
paragraphs: In one dimension, a signed quadratic model is $F_d=-c|v|v$ for c>0 and stationary fluid. If v is positive, the force is negative; if v is negative, the force is positive. Writing -cv² for every signed velocity would incorrectly keep drag in one direction during an upward launch.

The coefficient c has units kg/m because force divided by velocity squared gives that unit. In an aerodynamic form, $c=\rho C_dA/2$, where rho is fluid density, A is reference area, and Cd is a dimensionless coefficient. The complete c is dimensional even though Cd is not.

For positive downward terminal velocity with no buoyancy, mg-cvT²=0 gives $v_T=\sqrt{mg/c}$. The positive root satisfies the signed force law. A negative root of the squared equation does not describe an upward terminal state under downward gravity: at negative velocity, both drag and gravity point down.

At fixed c and g, quadratic terminal speed scales with the square root of mass, while linear terminal speed scales directly with mass at fixed b. The exponential solution derived above belongs to the linear law; it cannot simply be reused with a quadratic coefficient. Choose and justify the force law before solving its differential equation.

sections.heading: Handle zero drag by returning to the original equation
paragraphs: The expressions mg/b and m/b require b>0. Setting b=0 directly in them divides by zero. The original equation remains valid and becomes dv/dt=g. Its solution is $v=v_0+gt$ and $y=y_0+v_0t+gt^2/2$. For g>0 there is no finite terminal velocity.

For small positive b over a fixed short interval, the drag solution approaches that no-drag motion. Expanding the exponential shows the cancellation: 1-e^(-t/τ) is approximately t/τ minus t²/(2τ²), so release from rest gives v approximately gt and y approximately gt²/2. Taking this limit differs from substituting zero into an invalid quotient.

If both b and g are zero, every constant initial velocity solves the equation. There is no unique velocity selected by damping. The investigation asks for none as the selected terminal velocity and time constant in the zero-drag case, while still computing the valid velocity and position.

In the investigation, first predict vT, τ, final velocity, and final acceleration. Compare release from rest, an upward launch, and a launch above terminal velocity. Check a table row with mg+Fd=ma, compare equal t/τ across parameters, and finally set b=0. All plots have equivalent tables and keyboard controls; save your reasoning and the limitations in lesson notes.

examples.title: Derive and check a falling body's transient
examples.prompt: A 2 kg body is released from rest in stationary fluid. Linear drag has b=1 kg/s, g=10 m/s², and downward is positive. Find velocity and acceleration after 4 s, neglecting buoyancy and contact.

steps.reason: The force balance supplies the equilibrium value and the decay time without assuming constant acceleration.
Apply v(0)=0 and differentiate the resulting velocity law.
Four seconds is two time constants, not the exact end of the transient.
The independent force residual matches mass times acceleration to the shown rounding.

examples.conclusion: After 4 s, the body moves downward at about 17.293 m/s and still accelerates downward at about 1.353 m/s². Nonzero drag has reduced acceleration below g.

examples.title: Approach terminal velocity from above
examples.prompt: Use the same m=2 kg, b=1 kg/s, and g=10 m/s², but launch the body downward at 30 m/s. Find its velocity and acceleration after 2 s.

steps.reason: The initial difference from equilibrium is positive, so it must decay from above.
After one time constant, the difference has been multiplied by 1/e.
The velocity derivative is negative. Upward acceleration slows the body's downward motion.

examples.conclusion: Velocity stays above 20 m/s for every finite time in the exact model and decreases toward it. Terminal velocity is not a maximum allowed initial speed.

examples.title: Track an upward launch through zero velocity
examples.prompt: A 2 kg body starts at v0=-10 m/s with downward positive, b=1 kg/s, and g=10 m/s². Find when it reverses direction and compare initial and reversal acceleration.

steps.reason: Initially drag points downward, adding to gravity because the body moves upward.
The positive logarithmic time identifies the velocity crossing.
Drag vanishes at the instantaneous stop, but gravity does not.

examples.conclusion: The body reverses after about 0.811 s. Zero velocity at that instant is not terminal motion: acceleration is still 10 m/s² downward.

examples.title: Distinguish a target fraction from accumulated displacement
examples.prompt: For release from rest with vT=20 m/s and τ=2 s, find the time to reach 90% of terminal velocity and the downward displacement after 4 s.

steps.reason: A velocity fraction determines the remaining exponential fraction.
Integrate the changing velocity; do not multiply terminal velocity by the full elapsed time.
Differentiation independently checks the integrated displacement formula.

examples.conclusion: The 90% target occurs after about 4.605 s. Displacement at 4 s is about 45.413 m, less than the 80 m that would require terminal motion from the start.

examples.title: Audit two plausible but incomplete solutions
examples.prompt: A 3 kg body with b=1.5 kg/s and g=10 m/s² is released from rest. Assess the candidates vA(t)=20(1-e^(-t)) and vB(t)=20-15e^(-t/2), with SI units implicit in the numerical coefficients.

steps.reason: Both candidates use the correct equilibrium velocity, but that alone does not validate them.
Candidate A starts from rest but has the wrong decay rate and fails the differential equation.
Candidate B satisfies the differential equation but violates the stated initial condition.
The required transient coefficient cancels vT at t=0, while the decay rate is b/m.

examples.conclusion: Neither original candidate solves the complete initial-value problem. Check the equation and the initial state separately.

examples.title: Keep quadratic drag signed in both directions
examples.prompt: A 2 kg body has quadratic drag Fd=-c|v|v with c=0.5 kg/m in stationary fluid, g=10 m/s², and downward positive. Find its positive terminal velocity and drag during an upward velocity of -3 m/s.

steps.reason: Choose the positive root appropriate to downward terminal motion.
The absolute value preserves the speed factor while the signed velocity sets direction.
During the upward motion, drag and gravity both point down. The linear-drag exponential is not being assumed.

examples.conclusion: The terminal velocity is 2sqrt(10) m/s downward. At the specified upward velocity, drag is 4.5 N downward and acceleration exceeds g.

examples.title: Remove drag without dividing by zero
examples.prompt: Set b=0 in the original vertical force equation. Let g=10 m/s², v0=-4 m/s, y0=0, and downward be positive. Find the state after 2 s.

steps.reason: The original equation remains valid when drag is absent.
Integrate constant acceleration with the supplied signed initial velocity.
The signed displacement includes an initial upward part followed by downward motion.

examples.conclusion: Velocity is 16 m/s downward and displacement is 12 m downward. There is no finite terminal velocity under constant positive gravity with no drag; mg/b and m/b cannot be evaluated at b=0.

guided.title: Check a linear-drag prediction against its force equation
guided.setup: A 1 kg body is released from rest in stationary fluid, with b=0.5 kg/s, g=10 m/s², downward positive, and no buoyancy or contact. Predict the state after 2 s.
before: Force balance gives vT=mg/b and the decay time is τ=m/b.
For release from rest, v=vT(1-exp(-t/τ)) and a=g exp(-t/τ).
Calculate the exponential, enter decimals to at least three places, and check that mg-bv=ma.

question.prompt: Find terminal velocity, time constant, velocity and acceleration after 2 s, then interpret terminal motion.

fields.label: Velocity after 2 s
fields.help: Enter a calculated decimal to at least three places; absolute tolerance is 0.0005 m/s.

fields.label: Acceleration after 2 s
fields.help: Enter a calculated decimal to at least three places; absolute tolerance is 0.0005 m/s².

options.label: The body eventually stops because terminal means motion ends
options.feedback: The selected terminal velocity is positive. Position keeps changing while the force sum and acceleration approach zero.

options.label: Weight and drag balance at a nonzero constant downward velocity
options.feedback: At 20 m/s, the 10 N downward weight balances 10 N upward drag. Acceleration is zero while motion continues.

options.label: Terminal velocity is reached exactly after one time constant
options.feedback: After one time constant, about 36.8% of the initial difference remains. A nonzero transient approaches zero asymptotically.

hints: Velocity is about 12.642411 m/s and acceleration about 3.678794 m/s². Terminal motion means balanced nonzero forces, not zero velocity.
explanation: The selected terminal velocity is 20 m/s and the time constant is 2 s. One time constant gives v≈12.642411 m/s and a≈3.678794 m/s².
The force check is 10−0.5(12.642411)≈3.678794 N, matching the 1 kg mass times acceleration.
At terminal motion, drag is -10 N and weight is +10 N. The body continues downward at 20 m/s in this ideal model.
question.answerSummary: vT=20 m/s; τ=2 s; v(2)≈12.642411 m/s; a(2)≈3.678794 m/s²; terminal motion has balanced forces and nonzero velocity.

guided.after: One time constant determines a remaining fraction, not an exact settling time. Check whether a claimed solution satisfies both its initial condition and its force equation.

interaction.prompt: Predict the selected terminal velocity, time constant, final velocity, and final acceleration. Compare release from rest, an upward launch, and a launch above terminal velocity, then investigate the zero-drag boundary.

summary: State the axis, fluid velocity, coefficient law, and omitted forces. Drag opposes relative motion through the fluid.
For positive linear coefficient b, m dv/dt=mg-bv has terminal velocity mg/b and time constant m/b.
The solution v=vT+(v0-vT)exp(-t/τ) retains the initial state and approaches the same equilibrium from above or below.
Verify both the differential equation and initial conditions; either can fail independently.
Integrate the full velocity law for position and preserve the position initial condition.
One time constant removes about 63.2% of the initial velocity difference. A nonzero exact transient does not vanish at a finite time.
Quadratic drag uses -c|v|v, with coefficient units kg/m and positive terminal velocity sqrt(mg/c) under the stated assumptions.
At b=0, use the original equation and constant-acceleration solution. Do not divide by zero in formulas derived for positive drag.
retrieval: For m=2 kg, b=1 kg/s, g=10 m/s², and v0=30 m/s downward, find vT, τ, initial acceleration, and the remaining velocity difference after two time constants. Check after working: vT=20 m/s, τ=2 s, a(0)=-5 m/s², and the remaining difference is 10e^-2≈1.353353 m/s. Velocity then is about 21.353353 m/s, still above terminal velocity. If b becomes zero instead, acceleration is +10 m/s² and no finite terminal velocity is selected.
